title: Income from affiliates and joint ventures
subtitle: Equity method (20-50%) versus consolidation (>50%)
openingQuestion: When is an investment accounted for under the equity method rather than consolidated?
openingOptions: When ownership is 20-50%, or there is significant influence
Only when 100% of the company's charter capital is owned
explanation: A company with significant influence is usually accounted for under the equity method; majority control is what triggers consolidation into the financial statements. The 20-50% ownership band is the accounting convention for significant influence - above 50% is normally treated as control and requires the subsidiary's full financial statements to be consolidated.

realWorldExample.company: Profit recorded, cash not necessarily received
realWorldExample.description: This is the most easily missed feature of the equity method. When an associate reports a profit, the parent records its proportional share in profit for that period - but the cash only actually arrives when the associate decides to pay a dividend, and the parent cannot control that decision because it holds under 50%. The result is that a business can record hundreds of billions of associate profit over several years while the cash actually received is a small fraction of it. Comparing profit against operating cash flow, this is often one of the causes of the gap.

quiz.question: Why is equity income not quite the same as core operating revenue?
options: Because it never comes with any cash reaching the parent company
Because equity income is recorded on a cash basis
Because equity income is always negative at newly formed associates
Because it is a share of profit, not revenue from selling anything
quiz.explanation: Profit from affiliates and JVs is a share of someone else's profit, not sales revenue from the core business.

quiz.question: A company's net income has risen sharply, mostly from a one-off jump in equity income at a large joint venture. What should an investor do?
options: Separate the equity income and ask whether the growth repeats
Treat this as a sign the core business is growing sustainably
Conclude the company is dressing up the numbers to lift the share price
Ignore it, since equity income is always a very small proportion
quiz.explanation: Equity income depends on the associate's own operations, can swing unpredictably, and does not reflect the health of the main business - separating it out lets an investor judge how durable the profit really is.

quiz.question: Why can profit recorded under the equity method come with no cash at all?
options: Because the associate always retains all its profit to reinvest
Because the cash only arrives when the associate declares a dividend
Because accounting does not permit recording cash from an associate
Because this profit is taxed twice before it can be received
quiz.explanation: Recording profit in proportion to ownership is a bookkeeping entry. Cash only arises on a dividend, and at under 50% ownership the parent cannot decide that itself.

quiz.question: What is the biggest difference between consolidation and the equity method on the balance sheet?
options: The two methods produce identical results on the balance sheet
The equity method also records the associate's revenue
Consolidation brings the subsidiary's whole debt onto the balance sheet
Consolidation does not record the subsidiary's assets on the balance sheet
quiz.explanation: This is why ownership around the 50% threshold matters so much to an analyst: for the same underlying business, the debt may or may not appear on the consolidated balance sheet.

quiz.question: Why should profit from associates not be included in EBITDA for valuation?
options: Because it is already after tax, so including it double-counts the tax
Because accounting standards forbid adding any third-party profit into EBITDA
Because this item is always one-off and never repeats in later periods
Because it does not come from operations the business itself runs
quiz.explanation: EBITDA measures the operations the business controls, while associate profit comes from another company and usually brings no cash until a dividend is paid. The clean treatment is to exclude it from EBITDA and value that shareholding separately.

keyTakeaways: Equity income needs reading separately from core operating profit

summary.commonMistake: Easy to miss: above 50% usually moves to consolidation
summary.action: Equity income needs reading separately from core operating profit

sections.text: When a group owns part of another company (a joint venture, an associate), the profit received from it is recorded quite differently from ordinary sales revenue.
The equity method - significant influence without control

Where 20-50% of another company is owned (the accounting convention for significant influence), the investment is usually accounted for under the equity method - the parent records its proportional share of profit, known as equity income. Above 50% ownership (control), the subsidiary's whole financial statements must be consolidated, not merely its share of profit recorded.

items: Equity income is a share of an associate's profit, not sales revenue from core operations
20-50% ownership usually corresponds to significant influence (equity method); above 50% usually moves to consolidation
If net income rises sharply mostly on a jump in equity income, separate it out to judge how durable the profit is

sections.title: Three ownership levels, three treatments
sections.subtitle: The thresholds are an accounting convention; the substance is the degree of influence and control

concepts.def: Usually carried at cost or fair value. Income is recorded only on receiving a dividend or on sale.
Records the proportional share of profit in the income statement, with the carrying value of the investment on the balance sheet moving accordingly.
Brings the subsidiary's entire revenue, costs, assets and liabilities into the consolidated statements, then strips out the portion not owned as minority interest.

left.label: The equity method
left.text: The associate's revenue does NOT appear in the parent's revenue. Only a single line of profit is recorded. The associate's debt is likewise absent from the consolidated balance sheet.

right.label: Consolidation
right.text: The subsidiary's entire revenue, costs, assets and DEBT enter the consolidated statements, even where the parent owns only 51%. The unowned portion is separated out as minority interest.

sections.text: Three questions when associate profit is large

items: What percentage of profit after tax is it? Above 20-30% and the core operations are no longer the main story.
Is it stable across the years, or does it come from a one-off event at the associate?
How much dividend was actually received from the associates against the profit recorded? A large and persistent gap needs explaining.

lines: Not every dong of profit comes from the main business.
Separating out equity income gives you an accurate view of the core business's health.

practicePrompt.question: Business A holds 35% of the voting shares in company B. Which accounting method must A apply in its financial statements?
options: The equity method
Full consolidation of 100% of B's assets and liabilities into A
No recording of any item until B declares a dividend
Recording B as a short-term savings deposit
practicePrompt.explanation: Where 20% to 50% of the shares are owned (an associate or joint venture), the business applies the equity method. Only above 50% does consolidation apply.
